beats.beat: Judith Vane, having pieced the misunderstanding together from what she overheard, calls on Margaret and quietly explains that Dene's words meant ending the pretence, not his feeling for her.
Margaret goes at once to find Dene, and the two are discovered unmistakably close and sincere by Mrs Ferris and Mrs Pike arriving together at the schoolroom door.
Mrs Ferris asks Dene plainly whether he would marry Margaret with not a shilling of her aunt's money attached to her.

Dene says he would rather have Margaret penniless and honestly his than owe the marriage to anyone's fortune, an answer Mrs Ferris had not expected from a poor man, and she is satisfied something real has happened.

turn.note: Mrs Ferris's satisfaction converts the false engagement into one she will now actively support, which sets up chapter 5's settlement and banns.

problems: "He had her hand by then, and she had let him take it, and neither of them heard the latch" coordinates three clauses that shift subject each time (He / she / neither of them) and loses its thread partway.

listenability: "He had her hand by then, and she had let him take it, and neither of them heard the latch" is a three-clause chain with changing grammatical subject; split after "take it."

generic_prose.quote: She had put that question to three men in her life and had never before had it answered so fast.
generic_prose.replace_with: Name or specify the circumstance of one of those three men so the line belongs to Mrs Ferris's own history rather than reading as any wealthy widow's generic backstory.

trope_note: Delivers the compromising situation straight (the hand-holding discovery) and advances the false engagement toward a real one, with Mrs Pike's meddling given its payoff of being half-right for the wrong reasons.
fixes: Split "He had her hand by then, and she had let him take it, and neither of them heard the latch" into two sentences at "take it."

The chapter runs well over target (roughly 560 words against 450). Trim Judith's second speech ("You need not answer me... once in three") to a single sentence — the gossip-context is already established by Mrs Pike's visibility in chapter 3.
Compress Judith's explanation beat ("He said he had had the good of it... wrong end of it") — the first two sentences make the point; the third and fourth restate it.
Tighten Mrs Ferris's question in segment 23 — "where you stand" and "now or at my death" can both go without losing the force of the challenge.
Replace the generic aside about "three men in her life" with one concrete detail (a name, a year, a sum) so it reads as Mrs Ferris's history rather than any widow's.
